metaData.title: Atlantic Shipwrights Guild support follow up

sentences.text: Hi Garrett, thanks for taking the call.
This is the follow up I promised after the tickets you raised around the summer festival series.
I would like to understand what actually happened on the ground rather than what the tickets say, because the two are usually different.
Hello Elena. Happy to go through it properly.
The tickets were written at half past six in the morning by someone who had been awake since four, so I would not read too much into the wording.
Understood. Start me at the beginning. What does the autumn series actually consist of?
We run four regional gatherings between September and November, one in each of our chapters.
Each one is a day and a half, usually at a working boatyard, with demonstrations in the morning and member sessions in the afternoon.
They are small by most standards. Between three hundred and six hundred people at each.
And people arrive across the morning rather than all at once?
Mostly between seven thirty and nine, because the first demonstration starts at nine sharp and nobody misses it.
So it is a concentrated hour and a half rather than a steady trickle.
Give me a bit of background while we are here, because I have read your account notes and they are thin.
How big is the guild and how is it organised?
Just over four thousand members across four chapters on the eastern seaboard, from Maine down to the Chesapeake.
About two thirds are working boatbuilders and shipwrights, and the rest are what we politely call enthusiasts, who are often the ones with the money.
The guild is a hundred and nine years old and there are people who will tell you, at length, what it was like in the nineteen sixties.
A hundred and nine years of institutional memory is a mixed blessing in my experience.
It is exactly that. It gives us an archive nobody else has and a standards body that genuinely means something in the trade.
It also gives us four chapters who each believe their way of running a gathering is the correct one, and three of them are wrong.
I will not tell you which three because two of the chairs listen to these recordings.
I will not ask. How many staff do you have?
Six full time and two part time, which for four thousand members is lean but workable.
Almost everything at a gathering is run by volunteers, and we have about four hundred who do something in a given year.
My own job is mostly making sure the volunteers are equipped and then getting out of the way.
That is a good description of programme management generally.
It took me four years to learn it. My first two gatherings I tried to run everything myself and both of them were worse for it.
Walk me through how you handle the arrivals.
We set up the attendee kiosk on two laptops at the yard gate with a printer for badges.
That is the name we have always used for it, from the platform we were on before you acquired them, and honestly the whole guild still calls it that.
I know your documentation uses a different word but I have given up trying to retrain four hundred volunteers.
You do not need to retrain anyone on my account. I will use your word.
So what went wrong at the September gathering?
The yard has one connection and it goes through a single radio link to the road, which is fine right up until it is not.
If the hall wifi cuts out halfway through the morning, the attendee kiosk has to carry on signing people in and catch up later.
That morning it went out at eight ten and came back at eight fifty, which is the worst forty minutes it could have picked.

Our insurance requires us to show who was on site and roughly when, so the attendee kiosk staying up through an outage and reconciling afterwards is the difference between a compliant record and a gap.
What did the two people on the laptops do for those forty minutes?
One of them drove to the top of the lane and stood on a wall with a phone hotspot, which worked for about ten minutes before the battery gave out.
The other one wrote names on a clipboard.
Neither of those was planned, it is simply what people improvise at the gate.
And afterwards, how did the clipboard names get back into the system?
Two volunteers typed them in over the following week, twenty six names between them.
They worked from the clipboard and from a photograph somebody took of it, which was legible enough.
That insurance point is the part I had not understood from the ticket, and it is the part that will make this land.
Can I quote you on it?
Quote me on all of it. I have nothing to hide and I would rather it was said plainly.
Since we have covered the gatherings, tell me how the membership side is going.
Your renewal is in January if I remember the account correctly.
End of January, and I am not expecting any difficulty.
Membership is up about three percent this year, which for a heritage trade body is close to miraculous.
The apprenticeship programme is the reason. Every apprentice becomes a member and most of them stay.
Is the dues structure the same across the four chapters?
The national dues are the same and each chapter adds its own supplement, which ranges from nothing to forty dollars.
The chapter with the forty dollar supplement also runs the best programme, and funnily enough nobody complains about it.
The one that charges nothing has the highest churn, which is not the lesson anybody expected.
People value what they pay for, apparently.
Or they value what somebody bothers to organise, and the supplement is what pays for the bothering.
I think it is the second one, but I hold the view loosely because it is one chapter and one year.
How do the standards and certification pieces sit against membership?
We publish the construction standards that a good part of the trade works to, and about six hundred members hold a guild certification on top of their membership.
The certification is voluntary and it is renewed every five years with evidence of continued practice.
It matters most to the members who work on historic vessels, because the grant funders for that work ask for it by name.
Is there any prospect of a better connection at the yards themselves?
Not really. Two of the four are on working waterfronts where the infrastructure is sixty years old and nobody is going to dig it up for us.
We have looked at satellite units and the cost per gathering is more than the catering budget.
Then planning around the connection rather than relying on it is the only sensible answer.
That is where we have landed too.
We are a guild of people who build wooden boats. We are quite comfortable with the idea that the weather will not cooperate.
Tell me about the apprenticeship programme. It came up in one of your tickets and I did not follow the reference.
It is the thing I am proudest of and it is four years old now.
We place about thirty apprentices a year with member yards, on a two year structured programme with a logbook and assessed milestones.
The yards take them on properly, with wages, and the guild does the assessment and the paperwork so that a small yard is not put off by the administration.
Thirty a year against a trade that size is a significant proportion of the intake.
It is close to a fifth of all new entrants to the trade on this coast, according to the one piece of research anybody has done.
Nineteen of the first cohort of twenty two are still in the trade four years on, which is well ahead of our own forecast.
The three who left all went into boat repair for the marine insurance side, so arguably we did not lose them at all.
How is it funded?
A mix. Member yards pay a placement fee, two maritime trusts fund the assessment side, and one state has a skills grant we qualify for.
The funding is the fragile part, because the state grant is renewed annually and nobody will tell us anything about it until March.
So every year we plan a cohort we are not certain we can pay for, and every year so far it has worked out.
Does any of the logbook and milestone tracking sit in the system we host for you?
The enrolment and the member records do. The logbook itself is on paper, because the apprentices are in sheds with wet hands and a paper logbook survives that better than anything with a screen.
That is a deliberate choice rather than a limitation, and the assessors prefer it too.
Let me move on to the member workshops, since I have you.
How is the enrolment side running this term?
Fine, and that is a genuine fine rather than a polite one.
We have thirty one workshops running this term across the four chapters, with an average of fourteen people in each.
Enrolment opened in July and filled in about three weeks.
Any trouble with the materials lists and the deposits?
No. Deposits ran the same way as last term.
The materials lists we keep outside the system because they change with what timber we can get, and that is our choice rather than a limitation of yours.
Good. And your volunteer coordinators, are they set up with the access they need?
Three of the four are. The fourth chapter appointed a new coordinator in August and I have not got round to it.
I have the instructions from last time and I will do it this week.
Last area from me. How do you train the four hundred volunteers?
Badly, historically. For years it was whoever did it last time showing whoever is doing it this time, in a car park, ten minutes before the gates opened.
Two years ago we wrote it all down properly into eleven short guides, none longer than two pages, and we send them out a fortnight before each gathering.
It has made a noticeable difference and it cost one person three weeks of work.
Two pages is about the right length for something somebody will read standing up.
That was the rule we set ourselves. If it does not fit on two sides it is not a guide, it is a manual, and nobody reads a manual at seven in the morning.
We also made every guide start with the three things that go wrong most often, rather than with a description of the software.
That is better documentation practice than most software companies manage.
I will take the compliment.
It came out of watching people rather than out of any theory. We stood at the gate for a whole morning and wrote down every question anybody asked.
Forty one questions, of which eleven accounted for most of them, and those eleven became the guides.
Would you be willing to let me show those to our own documentation team?
Happily, as long as nobody minds that they are written in the language of a boatyard.
I will send those this afternoon, and I will offer a short session for the new coordinator if she would like one.
Thirty minutes, whenever suits her.
She would take you up on that. She is thorough and she will ask you better questions than I do.
Then to summarise: I am writing up the offline request with your insurance point attached, and offering a session to the new coordinator.
I will update the ticket with both so you have it in writing.
That covers it. Thanks Elena, that was more useful than the tickets.
